note: Shammai and Hillel disagreed over whether grapes harvested for the winepress can become ritually impure. Hillel challenged Shammai: why harvest grapes in purity but not olives? Shammai answered that if Hillel provoked him, he would decree impurity on olives too. A sword was stuck into the study hall and it was announced that anyone could enter but no one could leave. That day Hillel sat bowed before Shammai like a student, and the Gemara says it was as hard for Israel as the day the Golden Calf was made. Shammai and Hillel issued the decree and the people did not accept it; their students later issued it and the people accepted it.
why: The Gemara is counting the eighteen decrees the Sages passed on one famous day and needs to complete the tally. The decree about harvested grapes is given as another of the eighteen; afterward the Gemara asks what the reason for that decree was.

people.name: Hillel
people.about: Head of the Sages in his day; here he argued against the decree and was forced to sit before Shammai like a student.

people.name: Shammai
people.about: Hillel's colleague and opponent, who held that harvested grapes become susceptible to impurity and threatened to extend the decree to olives.

terms.meaning: In Jewish purity law, food can only become ritually impure after it has been moistened by certain liquids. The question is whether juice seeping from grapes during harvest counts.
Using ritually pure vessels and hands, so that the produce stays pure.
The idol the Israelites made in the desert (Exodus 32), remembered as one of the worst days in the nation's history.

note: Rabbi Zeira wanted to move from Babylonia to the Land of Israel, but his teacher Rav Yehuda held that leaving Babylonia for the Land of Israel violates a commandment, so Rabbi Zeira was avoiding him. Before leaving he decided to go and hear one more teaching from him. He found Rav Yehuda in the bathhouse telling his servant: bring me natron, bring me a comb, open your mouths and let out air, and drink from the bathhouse water. Rabbi Zeira said that had he come only to hear this, it would have been enough.
why: The Gemara has been discussing proper conduct while bathing. After the story it draws lessons from each of Rav Yehuda's instructions, such as that ordinary matters may be spoken in Hebrew in a bathhouse and why drinking hot water while bathing is healthy.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Rav Yehuda's student, who wanted to emigrate to the Land of Israel against his teacher's view.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rabbi Zeira's teacher, who held it was forbidden to leave Babylonia for the Land of Israel.

terms.meaning: A natural mineral salt used as soap for washing.

note: After bloodletting, Shmuel, Rav Yehuda and Rabba each needed a fire to keep warm. For Shmuel they broke up a teak armchair, for Rav Yehuda an ebony table, and for Rabba a bench, to use as fuel. Abaye asked Rabba whether breaking the bench did not violate the commandment 'Do not destroy'. Rabba answered that not destroying his own body mattered more to him.
why: Shmuel has ruled that a fire may be made on Shabbat for someone who let blood and caught cold, even in midsummer. These cases show how seriously the Sages took the danger of cold after bloodletting, even burning valuable furniture.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage for whom a teak armchair was broken up for a fire after bloodletting.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage for whom an ebony table was broken up for a fire.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage for whom a bench was broken up; he defended it to Abaye.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rabba's student, who asked whether breaking the bench was wasteful destruction.

terms.meaning: Drawing blood from the body as a medical treatment, common in ancient times. The person was considered weakened and at risk afterward.
A Torah prohibition (Deuteronomy 20:19) against needlessly destroying useful or valuable things.

note: Ablat, a gentile scholar, found Shmuel lying in the sun. He asked him, Wise man of the Jews, can something harmful become good? Shmuel answered that on a day of bloodletting the sun is good for a person. The Gemara comments that this was not really so: there is one day in the year when the sun is beneficial, the day of the summer solstice, and Shmuel did not want to reveal that remedy to Ablat.
why: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak has just advised that someone who let blood and has nothing to eat should lie in the sun. The story shows Shmuel doing so, and the Gemara adds that his stated reason was a cover.

people.name: Ablat
people.about: A gentile scholar who found Shmuel lying in the sun and questioned him.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage, called by Ablat the wise man of the Jews.

terms.meaning: Drawing blood from the body as a medical treatment; the person was considered weakened afterward and needed warmth and food.
The summer solstice, the longest day of the year, which falls around the Hebrew month of Tammuz.

note: When Rabbi Hanina's daughter died, he did not cry over her. His wife asked him whether he had merely let a chicken out of the house. He answered that if he cried he would suffer twice: from the loss and from blindness. The Gemara explains that he followed a teaching that some tears are bad for the eyes, among them tears of crying out of grief.
why: The discussion has just cited Shmuel's statement that after age forty, tears permanently weaken the eyesight. Rabbi Hanina's refusal to weep for his daughter puts that belief into practice.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage who did not weep when his daughter died, for fear of losing his sight.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who reported the teaching about good and bad tears.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Ketzarta
people.about: The Sage in whose name Rabbi Yohanan taught that there are six kinds of tears.
